{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_01Rj7FQ4ShzKcne9oCs594gs","type":"tool_result","content":"     1→# apiserver Architecture\n     2→\n     3→## 1. Server Composition\n     4→\n     5→The `kube-apiserver` binary is not one server, but a **server chain** of three distinct\n     6→`GenericAPIServer` instances: the core Kubernetes API, API extensions (CRDs), and the aggregation\n     7→layer.\n     8→\n     9→This composition is managed by a layered configuration system, starting with command-line\n    10→flags parsed by `options` structs (e.g., `RecommendedOptions` in `pkg/server/options`), which\n    11→populate a `Config` object that is then used to instantiate the `GenericAPIServer`\n    12→instances. The construction of this delegation chain can be found in the `CreateServerChain`\n    13→function in `cmd/kube-apiserver/app/server.go`.\n    14→\n    15→```mermaid\n    16→graph TD\n    17→    subgraph Incoming Request\n    18→        direction LR\n    19→        A[User/Client] --> B{/apis/apps/v1/deployments};\n    20→    end\n    21→\n    22→    subgraph kube-apiserver process\n    23→        direction LR\n    24→        B --> C[Aggregator Server];\n    25→        C -- Not an APIService --> D[Kube API Server];\n    26→        D -- Handles Request --> E[REST Storage];\n    27→        C -- Is an APIService --> F[Proxy to Extension API Server];\n    28→        D -- Not a Core API --> G[API Extensions Server];\n    29→        G -- Handles CRD --> E;\n    30→    end\n    31→```\n    32→\n    33→1.  **Aggregator Server (`kube-aggregator`):**\n    34→    *   **Purpose:** Handles the `apiregistration.k8s.io` API and acts as a reverse proxy for\n    35→        extension API servers. This functionality was designed to allow third-party APIs to be\n    36→        \"aggregated\" into the main Kubernetes API server seamlessly.\n    37→    *   **Mechanism:** It watches `APIService` objects. When a request arrives (e.g., for\n    38→        `/apis/mycompany.com/v1/myresources`), it checks if an `APIService` has \"claimed\"\n    39→        that path. If so, it uses a `ServiceResolver` to find the IP of the backing\n    40→        `Service` and proxies the request.\n    41→    *   **Use Case:** This pattern is for programmatic, high-control extensions that require\n    42→        custom business logic (e.g., non-CRUD subresources like `/logs`) or alternative\n    43→        storage backends.\n    44→    *   **Delegation:** If no `APIService` matches, it delegates the request to the next\n    45→        server in the chain.\n    46→\n    47→2.  **Kube API Server (Core):**\n    48→    *   **Purpose:** Serves all the built-in Kubernetes APIs (`core/v1`, `apps/v1`, etc.).\n    49→    *   **Mechanism:** This is the main server, configured with all the core REST storage\n    50→        strategies.\n    51→    *   **Delegation:** If a request is for a path that is not a core API (e.g., for a CRD),\n    52→        it delegates the request to the next server in the chain.\n    53→\n    54→3.  **API Extensions Server (`apiextensions-apiserver`):**\n    55→    *   **Purpose:** Handles the `apiextensions.k8s.io` API, which manages\n    56→        `CustomResourceDefinition` objects (CRDs). The evolution of CRDs from a simple extension\n    57→        mechanism to a feature-rich system with validation, versioning, and defaulting is\n    58→        documented in a series of KEPs, starting with the graduation to GA in Kubernetes v1.16.\n    59→    *   **Mechanism:** When a CRD is created, this server dynamically creates and installs a\n    60→        new REST storage handler for the new resource, making it immediately available.\n    61→    *   **Use Case:** CRDs are the most common extension pattern, offering a declarative,\n    62→        schema-based way to define new resource types that are stored in etcd and require no\n    63→        custom API server code.\n    64→    *   **Delegation:** It is the end of the chain. If it cannot handle a request, a `404 Not\n    65→        Found` is returned.\n    66→\n    67→## 2. Handler Chain\n    68→\n    69→Every request flows through a standard chain of HTTP handlers (filters). The request body\n    70→is not deserialized until it has passed authentication and authorization. The default handler\n    71→chain is constructed by the `DefaultBuildHandlerChain` function in\n    72→`staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server/config.go`.\n    73→\n    74→```mermaid\n    75→sequenceDiagram\n    76→    participant Client\n    77→    participant Handler Chain\n    78→    participant Authentication\n    79→    participant Authorization\n    80→    participant Priority and Fairness\n    81→    participant Admission Control\n    82→    participant REST Endpoint\n    83→\n    84→    Client->>Handler Chain: Request\n    85→    Handler Chain->>Authentication: Authenticate\n    86→    Authentication-->>Handler Chain: User Info\n    87→    Handler Chain->>Authorization: Authorize\n    88→    Authorization-->>Handler Chain: Allowed/Denied\n    89→    Handler Chain->>Priority and Fairness: Classify & Queue\n    90→    Priority and Fairness-->>Handler Chain: Proceed\n    91→    Handler Chain->>Admission Control: Mutate & Validate\n    92→    Admission Control-->>Handler Chain: Object OK\n    93→    Handler Chain->>REST Endpoint: Handle\n    94→    REST Endpoint-->>Handler Chain: Response\n    95→    Handler Chain-->>Client: Response\n    96→```\n    97→\n    98→The handler chain consists of the following stages:\n    99→\n   100→1.  **Authentication (`pkg/authentication`):** This filter identifies the user. The system is\n   101→    pluggable and composed of multiple authenticators (e.g., client certs, bearer tokens, OIDC).\n   102→    The identity of the user is determined by the first authenticator in the chain that successfully\n   103→    identifies the user.\n   104→2.  **Authorization (`pkg/authorization`):** This filter checks if the user is permitted to\n   105→    perform the action. This system is also pluggable and composed of multiple authorizers\n   106→    (e.g., RBAC, Node, Webhook). Each authorizer may respond with either allow, deny, or no opinion.\n   107→    If the response is no opinion, the request is passed to the next authorizer in the chain.\n   108→3.  **Priority and Fairness (`pkg/util/flowcontrol`):** This subsystem manages request\n   109→    concurrency, classifying requests into `FlowSchema`s and `PriorityLevel`s to prevent\n   110→    overload. This feature was introduced to prevent high traffic from overwhelming the API\n   111→    server and to ensure that critical cluster operations are not starved.\n   112→4.  **Admission Control (`pkg/admission`):** This is the primary mechanism for policy\n   113→    enforcement. It is only at this stage that the request body is deserialized into an\n   114→    object. It is a chain of plugins that can mutate or validate an object. The built-in Pod\n   115→    Security admission controller is a key example of this, enforcing Pod Security Standards\n   116→    at the namespace level.\n   117→5.  **REST Endpoint Handling (`pkg/endpoints`):** The request is finally dispatched to the\n   118→    appropriate REST handler, which is installed by the `APIInstaller`.\n   119→\n   120→## 3. API Group Registration\n   121→\n   122→The high-level steps for introducing an API are:\n   123→\n   124→1.  **Define Types:** Create or modify the Go structs in the `types.go` file for the API group.\n   125→2.  **Generate Code:** Use the code generators provided by the Kubernetes project to create the required\n   126→    boilerplate methods for deep-copy, conversion, and defaulting.\n   127→3.  **Implement the `Strategy`:** Write the custom business logic and validation for the\n   128→    resource in its `Strategy` object.\n   129→4.  **Register and Install:** Create the `APIGroupInfo` struct, bundling the `Scheme` and the\n   130→    `Strategy`-configured storage, and pass it to the `GenericAPIServer`'s `InstallAPIGroup`\n   131→    method.\n   132→\n   133→### The API Group Registry\n   134→\n   135→The `runtime.Scheme` acts as a central registry for an API group's type information. A single\n   136→`Scheme` object is created for each API group and is responsible for the following key\n   137→capabilities:\n   138→\n   139→*   **Type Registration and Mapping:** The `Scheme`'s primary role is to map a GroupVersionKind\n   140→    (GVK) to its corresponding Go type and back. This process also relies on the `deepcopy-gen`\n   141→    tool to create `DeepCopy()` methods for each type, which is critical for ensuring that\n   142→    objects returned from caches are never modified directly.\n   143→\n   144→*   **API Conversion:** The `Scheme` stores the conversion functions that translate objects\n   145→    between different API versions. These functions are typically generated by the\n   146→    `conversion-gen` tool and enable the **hub-and-spoke** model.\n   147→\n   148→*   **Defaulting:** The `Scheme` registers defaulting functions that populate optional fields in\n   149→    an object. These are usually generated by the `defaulter-gen` tool.\n   150→\n   151→*   **Declarative Validation:** The `Scheme` can store and execute code-generated validation\n   152→    functions, providing a baseline level of validation. This is distinct from the primary,\n   153→    handwritten business logic validation, which is handled by the `Strategy` object.\n   154→\n   155→### The `APIGroupInfo` Struct and `Strategy` Object\n   156→\n   157→With a populated `Scheme`, the API group is registered with the `GenericAPIServer` by bundling\n   158→the `Scheme` with the storage backend and versioning information into an `APIGroupInfo` struct.\n   159→\n   160→```mermaid\n   161→graph TD\n   162→    subgraph Server Configuration\n   163→        A[APIGroupInfo for apps v1];\n   164→        A --> B{Scheme: Knows Deployment v1};\n   165→        A --> C{Storage: deployments RESTStorage};\n   166→        A --> D{Version Priority: v1, v1beta1};\n   167→    end\n   168→\n   169→    subgraph RESTStorage Implementation\n   170→        C --> E[genericregistry.Store];\n   171→        E --> F[etcd client];\n   172→        E --> G[Deployment Strategy];\n   173→    end\n   174→\n   175→    subgraph Server Runtime\n   176→        H[GenericAPIServer] -- InstallAPIGroup --> I[APIInstaller];\n   177→        I -- Uses --> A;\n   178→        I --> J{Register /apis/apps/v1/deployments};\n   179→        J --> K[HTTP Handler];\n   180→        K -- On Request --> C;\n   181→    end\n   182→```\n   183→\n   184→The registration process follows these steps:\n   185→\n   186→1.  **`APIGroupInfo` Construction:** For each API group, an `APIGroupInfo` struct is created,\n   187→    which contains the populated `Scheme`, a map of resources to their storage\n   188→    implementations, and an ordered list of **Version Priority**.\n   189→\n   190→2.  **REST Storage Instantiation:** For each resource, a `genericregistry.Store` is created. It\n   191→    is configured with a resource-specific `Strategy` object that contains the core business\n   192→    logic (e.g., handwritten validation).\n   193→\n   194→3.  **API Group Installation:** The `GenericAPIServer`'s `InstallAPIGroup` method takes the\n   195→    `APIGroupInfo` and uses an `APIInstaller` to expose the resources as HTTP endpoints.\n   196→\n   197→## 4. Watch Cache\n   198→\n   199→To handle the high volume of watch requests from controllers without overwhelming etcd, the\n   200→apiserver uses a **watch cache**. The implementation can be found in\n   201→`staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/`.\n   202→\n   203→*   **Initialization:** The cacher first performs a `LIST` to get the current state of all\n   204→    objects and a `ResourceVersion` for that point-in-time. It then starts a `WATCH` from\n   205→    that version to ensure a consistent stream of events.\n   206→*   **Serving from Cache:** Most list and watch requests are served from this in-memory cache, which\n   207→    dramatically reduces the load on etcd. Consistent reads are also served from the\n   208→    cache. This is achieved by first fetching the revision number of the latest write from\n   209→    etcd. The server then ensures the cache is at least that recent—waiting for it to\n   210→    refresh if necessary—before serving the request.\n   211→*   **Fallback to Storage:** If a client request cannot be served from the\n   212→    cache's buffer, the request \"falls through\" to the underlying etcd storage.\n   213→*   **Bookmarks:** The cacher uses bookmark events to track the latest `ResourceVersion` for\n   214→    unchanged objects. This prevents the cache's `ResourceVersion` from becoming too old,\n   215→    which avoids the need for expensive relist operations from etcd when the objects have\n   216→    not been modified.\n   217→\n   218→## 5. Conflict Resolution\n   219→\n   220→*   **Optimistic Concurrency via `resourceVersion`:** Clients are expected to perform updates using a\n   221→    read-modify-write workflow. The apiserver uses the `resourceVersion` field of every\n   222→    object to enforce optimistic concurrency. This `resourceVersion` is not an arbitrary number;\n   223→    it maps directly to etcd's globally consistent `mod_revision`. When a client submits an\n   224→    update (`PUT` or `PATCH`), it must provide the `resourceVersion` of the object it based its\n   225→    modifications on. If the `resourceVersion` on the server does not match the current\n   226→    `mod_revision` in etcd, the server rejects the request with a `409 Conflict` error. This\n   227→    forces the client to re-read the object, resolve the conflict, and resubmit with the new\n   228→    `resourceVersion`.\n   229→*   **Server-Side Apply:** A declarative, \"intent-based\" patch. The server maintains a\n   230→    `managedFields` section in the object's metadata to track which \"manager\" (e.g., a\n   231→    controller) owns each field. This allows multiple actors to manage different parts of the\n   232→    same object without overwriting each other's changes.\n   233→\n   234→## 6. Discovery and OpenAPI\n   235→\n   236→Apiservers serve the `/apis` discovery endpoints and the `/openapi/v2` and `/openapi/v3`\n   237→specifications. The generation of the OpenAPI specification is a multi-stage process.\n   238→\n   239→*   **`openapi-gen`**: This tool reflects on Go structs, reads godoc comments, and looks at\n   240→    validation struct tags to generate a map of all API definitions.\n   241→*   **`zz_generated.openapi.go`**: The output is a large Go file containing a\n   242→    `GetOpenAPIDefinitions` function.\n   243→*   **Runtime**: The `GenericAPIServer` calls this generated function to build the final OpenAPI\n   244→    JSON spec that it serves to clients.\n   245→\n   246→## 7. Security & Observability\n   247→\n   248→*   **Audit (`pkg/audit`):** The apiserver has a policy-driven event logging pipeline. The audit\n   249→    policy controls what is logged and at which stage of a request.\n   250→*   **Security:**\n   251→    *   **mTLS:** The primary authentication mechanism for system components.\n   252→    *   **Service Account Token Issuance:** The `kube-apiserver` acts as an OIDC provider,\n   253→        issuing and validating JWTs for `ServiceAccount`s.\n   254→\n   255→## 8. Streaming Protocols\n   256→\n   257→*   **Websockets:** The apiserver uses websockets to upgrade HTTP\n   258→    connections for interactive, streaming protocols like `exec`, `attach`, and\n   259→    `port-forward`. The `UpgradeAwareProxyHandler` manages this process.\n   260→"}]},"parent_tool_use_id":"toolu_01QjGE52cKFYa1r9o1Ax6PA7","session_id":"43226105-e080-4119-a8ce-453f7cd5f406","uuid":"466dcc54-54ad-4a58-ab4b-b1df5c68b4ba"}

Subsystem Purpose and Boundaries\n\nThe `apiserver` library (`staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/`) is a reusable framework for building Kubernetes-style API servers. It provides the full HTTP request lifecycle—authentication, authorization, admission control, serialization, REST semantics, storage, and watch—as composable Go packages. The `kube-apiserver` binary is the primary consumer, but the library is intentionally decoupled so that projects like the aggregated API server, CRD API server, and custom API servers built with `apiserver-builder` can embed and extend it independently.\n\n### Boundaries\n\nThe library owns everything *between* the TLS listener and the etcd client. It does **not** own:\n\n- **Upstream:** TLS certificate management, load-balancer health probing, or network policy. These are external to the process.\n- **Downstream:** The etcd cluster itself. The library provides an etcd3 storage driver (`pkg/storage/etcd3/`) but treats etcd as a pluggable backend behind the `storage.Interface` abstraction (`pkg/storage/interfaces.go:169`).\n- **Peer concerns:** Controller logic, scheduler decisions, and kubelet communication. The API server library is strictly a data-plane gateway for the cluster's persisted state.\n\n### Upstream Dependencies\n\n| Dependency | Role |\n|---|---|\n| `k8s.io/apimachinery` | Shared type system (`runtime.Object`, `schema.GroupVersionKind`), serialization codecs, field selectors, label selectors |\n| `k8s.io/client-go` | Loopback client for self-referential operations (post-start hooks use `LoopbackClientConfig`) |\n| `go.etcd.io/etcd/client/v3` | etcd gRPC client used by `pkg/storage/etcd3/store.go` |\n| `github.com/emicklei/go-restful/v3` | HTTP routing framework for API group endpoints |\n| `k8s.io/kube-openapi` | OpenAPI v2/v3 spec generation and serving |\n\n### Downstream Consumers\n\nAny binary that calls `GenericAPIServer.InstallAPIGroups()` to register resources. The canonical example is `cmd/kube-apiserver`, but the library is also used by the aggregator (`kube-aggregator`) and sample API servers.\n\n---\n\n## 2. Key Components and Responsibility Split\n\nThe library decomposes into six major subsystems. Each has a clear responsibility boundary and communicates with neighbors through well-defined Go interfaces.\n\n### 2.1 Server Core (`pkg/server/`)\n\n**Responsibility:** Assembles the HTTP handler chain, manages server lifecycle (start, readiness, graceful shutdown), and provides the delegation mechanism for composing multiple API servers.\n\n**Key types:**\n\n- `GenericAPIServer` (`genericapiserver.go:109`): The central server struct. Holds the handler, admission controller, authorizer, post-start hooks, health checks, lifecycle signals, and the delegation target chain.\n- `Config` (`config.go:110`): Configuration for building a `GenericAPIServer`. Contains `BuildHandlerChainFunc`, authentication/authorization info, flow control settings, shutdown parameters, and the `RESTOptionsGetter` for storage configuration.\n- `APIServerHandler` (`handler.go:42`): Wraps three HTTP handler tiers: `FullHandlerChain` (all filters applied), `GoRestfulContainer` (API routes), and `NonGoRestfulMux` (non-API routes like `/healthz`, `/metrics`). The `Director` (`handler.go:115`) routes between the two backends.\n- `DelegationTarget` interface (`genericapiserver.go:308`): Enables chaining of multiple API servers (e.g., kube-apiserver delegates to aggregator delegates to apiextensions-server). Each delegate contributes its own hooks, health checks, and unprotected handlers.\n\n### 2.2 Filter Chain (`pkg/server/filters/`, `pkg/endpoints/filters/`)\n\n**Responsibility:** Implements the ordered chain of HTTP middleware that every request passes through before reaching the REST handler.\n\nThese are pure `http.Handler` wrappers composed in `DefaultBuildHandlerChain()` (`config.go:1015`). The chain is assembled inside-out (innermost handler wraps first), so the outermost filter in the source code is the first to execute at runtime.\n\nFilter files are split across two packages:\n- `pkg/server/filters/` — infrastructure filters (panic recovery, timeouts, flow control, CORS, GOAWAY)\n- `pkg/endpoints/filters/` — API-semantic filters (authentication, authorization, audit, impersonation, request info)\n\n### 2.3 Endpoint Handlers (`pkg/endpoints/`)\n\n**Responsibility:** Maps REST verbs to handler functions, installs API group routes into the go-restful container, and drives content negotiation.\n\n- `APIInstaller` (`installer.go:62`): Given an `APIGroupVersion` with a storage map, generates go-restful `WebService` routes for every resource. The central function `registerResourceHandlers()` (`installer.go:287`) introspects which `rest.*` interfaces each storage implements (e.g., `rest.Creater`, `rest.Lister`, `rest.Watcher`) and registers only the supported verbs.\n- Verb handlers in `pkg/endpoints/handlers/`: `GetResource()` / `ListResource()` (`get.go`), `CreateResource()` (`create.go`), `UpdateResource()` (`update.go`), `PatchResource()` (`patch.go`), `DeleteResource()` / `DeleteCollection()` (`delete.go`), `WatchServer` (`watch.go`).\n- Content negotiation (`handlers/negotiation/negotiate.go`): Matches `Accept` / `Content-Type` headers to registered serializers (JSON, YAML, Protobuf, CBOR).\n\n### 2.4 Admission Control (`pkg/admission/`)\n\n**Responsibility:** Runs pluggable mutation and validation logic on create, update, and delete operations after authentication and authorization but before persistence.\n\n- `Interface` / `MutationInterface` / `ValidationInterface` (`interfaces.go:123-144`): The core plugin interfaces. A plugin can implement mutation, validation, or both.\n- `chainAdmissionHandler` (`chain.go:23`): Chains multiple plugins. `Admit()` runs all mutating plugins in order, short-circuiting on error. `Validate()` runs all validating plugins and aggregates errors.\n- Admission is invoked inside endpoint handlers. For example, in `CreateResource()` (`create.go`), mutating admission runs at line ~203 via `mutatingAdmission.Admit()`, and validating admission is wired through `rest.AdmissionToValidateObjectFunc()`.\n\n### 2.5 Authentication & Authorization (`pkg/authentication/`, `pkg/authorization/`, `pkg/endpoints/filters/`)\n\n**Responsibility:** Establish caller identity and enforce access policy.\n\n- **Authentication filter** (`endpoints/filters/authentication.go:46`): `WithAuthentication()` calls `authenticator.Request.AuthenticateRequest()`, stores the resulting `user.Info` in the request context, and strips the `Authorization` header. If authentication fails, the request is forwarded to a `failedHandler` that returns 401.\n- **Authorization filter** (`endpoints/filters/authorization.go:53`): `WithAuthorization()` constructs `AttributesRecord` from the request info and user, calls `authorizer.Authorize()`, and returns 403 on `DecisionDeny` or `DecisionNoOpinion`. The `Authorizer` interface (`authorization/authorizer/interfaces.go:83`) returns a three-valued decision: `DecisionAllow`, `DecisionDeny`, `DecisionNoOpinion`.\n\n### 2.6 Storage Layer (`pkg/storage/`, `pkg/registry/`)\n\n**Responsibility:** Provides a key-value abstraction over etcd and an in-memory watch cache for serving list and watch requests efficiently.\n\n- `storage.Interface` (`storage/interfaces.go:169`): The backend contract. Methods: `Create`, `Delete`, `Watch`, `Get`, `GetList`, `GuaranteedUpdate`. Implementations do not know about Kubernetes resource semantics—they operate on opaque keys and `runtime.Object`.\n- `etcd3.store` (`storage/etcd3/store.go:80`): Direct etcd3 implementation. Handles codec transformations, lease management, and value encryption via a configurable `value.Transformer`.\n- `Cacher` (`storage/cacher/cacher.go:262`): In-memory cache that fronts the etcd3 store. Serves `Watch` and `List` from a ring-buffer `watchCache` populated by a `Reflector`. Mutations are delegated to the underlying `storage.Interface`. This is the component that makes watch scalable—without it, every watch would be a direct etcd watch, which does not scale past a few hundred concurrent watchers.\n- `Store` (`registry/generic/registry/store.go:100`): The generic REST storage implementation that most built-in resources embed. Implements CRUD by composing `storage.Interface` with resource-specific strategies (`RESTCreateStrategy`, `RESTUpdateStrategy`, `RESTDeleteStrategy`).\n- `StorageDecorator` (`registry/generic/storage_decorator.go:27`): A function type that wraps raw storage creation. The default decorator is `StorageWithCacher()` (`registry/generic/registry/storage_factory.go:36`), which wraps etcd3 storage with the `Cacher`.\n\n---\n\n## 3. The chain was assembled by `DefaultBuildHandlerChain()` (`config.go:1015`). Filters execute in the following order (outermost first at runtime):\n\n```\n1. The director iterates over registered `go-restful` WebServices. For our request path `/apis/apps/v1/namespaces/default/deployments`, it matches a WebService rooted at `/apis/apps/v1` and dispatches via `goRestfulContainer.Dispatch()` (`handler.go:145`).\n\nIf no WebService matches (e.g., `/healthz`, `/metrics`), the request falls through to `NonGoRestfulMux` (`handler.go:153`).\n\n### Phase 3: REST Handler Execution\n\nThe go-restful container matches the route to the handler installed by `registerResourceHandlers()` (`installer.go:287`). For a POST, this is `restfulCreateResource()` (`installer.go:1306`), which wraps `CreateResource()` (`create.go:245`).\n\nInside `CreateResource()`:\n\n1. **Decode the request body** (create.go, ~line 100-140): Uses the negotiated serializer based on `Content-Type`. The object is deserialized into an internal `runtime.Object`.\n\n2. **Default and validate** (via `CreateStrategy`): The `RESTCreateStrategy` interface (defined in `registry/rest/`) calls `PrepareForCreate`, `Validate`, and `Canonicalize` on the object.\n\n3. **Mutating admission** (~line 203): If the admission controller implements `MutationInterface`, `Admit()` is called. This runs the entire chain of mutating admission plugins (including webhooks) in sequence. Each plugin can modify the object.\n\n4. **Validating admission** (~line 188): `Validate()` runs all validating admission plugins. Errors from all plugins are aggregated and returned.\n\n5. **Field management** (via `FieldManager`, ~line 199): For server-side apply and managed-field tracking, the field manager updates ownership metadata.\n\n6. **Persist to storage**: The handler calls `rest.NamedCreater.Create()`, which resolves to `Store.Create()` (`registry/generic/registry/store.go`). The `Store` constructs the etcd key using `KeyFunc`, then calls `storage.Interface.Create()`.\n\n### Phase 4: Storage Write Path\n\n`storage.Interface.Create()` reaches either the `Cacher` or the raw `etcd3.store`, depending on the decorator.\n\nWhen using the standard `StorageWithCacher()` decorator:\n- **Create goes directly to etcd**: `Cacher` delegates mutations to the underlying `etcd3.store.Create()` (`storage/etcd3/store.go`). The etcd3 implementation encodes the object, applies any configured `value.Transformer` (e.g., encryption at rest), and issues an etcd `PUT` with a lease if TTL is specified.\n- **The Cacher's watch cache is updated asynchronously**: A separate goroutine running a `Reflector` watches etcd for changes and pushes events into the `Cacher.incoming` channel, which are then dispatched to all registered `cacheWatcher` instances.\n\n### Phase 5: Response Serialization\n\nAfter successful persistence, the handler serializes the created object using the negotiated output serializer, sets appropriate HTTP status (201 Created), and writes it to the `http.ResponseWriter`. The filter chain then unwinds—audit events are finalized, wait groups are decremented, and latency metrics are recorded.\n\n### Watch Flow (Variant)\n\nFor `GET /api/v1/pods?watch=true`, `ListResource()` (`get.go:171`) detects `opts.Watch == true` at line ~250, calls `rw.Watch()` on the storage to obtain a `watch.Interface`, and hands it to `serveWatchHandler()` (`watch.go:70`). This creates a `WatchServer` (`watch.go:188`) that enters a long-running loop (`HandleHTTP()`, watch.go:235):\n\n```\nfor {\n    select {\n    case event := <-watcher.ResultChan():\n        encode and flush event to HTTP response\n    case <-serverShuttingDown:\n        return\n    case <-ctx.Done():\n        return\n    case <-timeout:\n        return\n    }\n}\n```\n\nEvents arrive from `Cacher.Watch()`, which creates a `cacheWatcher` (`storage/cacher/cache_watcher.go:53`) that filters the shared event stream by the watch's predicate. This fan-out architecture means thousands of watchers share a single etcd watch per resource type.\n\n---\n\n## 4. Failure Modes, Limits, and Design Tradeoffs\n\n### 4.1 Watch Cache Consistency\n\nThe `Cacher` serves list and watch from an in-memory cache that lags behind etcd by an indeterminate amount. This is a deliberate tradeoff: serving from cache avoids overwhelming etcd with read traffic, but clients can observe stale data.\n\n**Mitigation:** The `ResourceVersion` mechanism provides consistency control. Clients can request `resourceVersion=0` (serve from cache, any version) or `resourceVersion=\"\"` (quorum read from etcd). The `Cacher` tracks the `incomingHWM` (high water mark, `cacher.go:266`) to determine the freshest version available in cache. Bookmark events (`cacheWatcher` states at `cache_watcher.go:37-49`) keep long-running watches informed of progress even when no real events occur.\n\n**Risk:** If the reflector falls behind or is disconnected, the cache may serve increasingly stale data. The `ready` flag (`cacher.go:280`) blocks reads during cache repopulation to prevent serving partial state.\n\n### 4.2 Admission Webhook Failure\n\nMutating and validating admission webhooks are external HTTP calls. If a webhook endpoint is unreachable:\n\n- **Fail-open vs. fail-closed** is configured per webhook via `failurePolicy`. A `Fail` policy rejects the request; an `Ignore` policy allows it to proceed without webhook evaluation.\n- **Timeout:** Webhooks have a configurable timeout (default 10s). A slow webhook blocks the entire request.\n\n**Tradeoff:** Fail-closed provides stronger policy enforcement but can cause cascading unavailability if the webhook backend is down—potentially blocking all mutations in the cluster. Fail-open preserves availability but allows policy violations to slip through.\n\n### 4.3 Request Timeout and Long-Running Requests\n\n`WithTimeoutForNonLongRunningRequests` (`filters/timeout.go:38`) enforces a deadline on regular requests. Long-running requests (watches, port-forwards, exec) are identified by `LongRunningFunc` (`filters/longrunning.go:28`) based on verb and subresource and are **exempted** from this timeout.\n\n**Tradeoff:** Timeout exemption for watches means a misbehaving watch can consume a connection and goroutine indefinitely. The `WithWatchTerminationDuringShutdown` filter (`filters/watch_termination.go:28`) addresses this during graceful shutdown by tracking watches in a wait group and terminating them after a grace period. The `WatchRequestWaitGroup` (`genericapiserver.go:228`) uses rate-limited termination to avoid thundering-herd reconnects.\n\n### 4.4 Priority and Fairness (APF) vs. Max-In-Flight\n\nThe server supports two concurrency control mechanisms, selected by whether `FlowControl` is configured (`config.go:1022-1031`):\n\n- **APF** (`filters/priority-and-fairness.go`): Classifies requests into FlowSchemas mapped to PriorityLevels, each with dedicated concurrency shares and queuing. This prevents a burst of low-priority requests (e.g., a runaway controller list-all) from starving high-priority requests (e.g., node heartbeats).\n- **Max-In-Flight** (`filters/maxinflight.go:126`): Simple counting semaphore with separate limits for mutating and read-only requests. No queuing—excess requests get 429.\n\n**Tradeoff:** APF provides fairness but adds complexity and latency (queue wait time). Max-In-Flight is simpler but provides no isolation between tenants or request classes.\n\n### 4.5 etcd Storage Pressure\n\nEvery mutating request results in an etcd write. The `GuaranteedUpdate` method (`storage/interfaces.go:243`) retries on conflict (stale `resourceVersion`), which can amplify write load under contention. The etcd3 store maintains leases for TTL objects and runs a compactor to reclaim space.\n\n**Limit:** etcd has a default 1.5 MB value size limit and a recommended database size of 8 GB. Large objects (e.g., very large ConfigMaps, deeply nested CRDs) can hit the value size limit. The `maxRequestBodyBytes` field on `GenericAPIServer` (`genericapiserver.go:238`) bounds request body sizes server-side.\n\n### 4.6 Graceful Shutdown Sequence\n\nThe shutdown flow (`genericapiserver.go:525-624`) is multi-phased:\n\n1. `stopCh` is closed → `ShutdownInitiated` signal fires → `/readyz` starts returning failure.\n2. `ShutdownDelayDuration` elapses → `AfterShutdownDelayDuration` signal fires → load balancers should have drained.\n3. Pre-shutdown hooks execute.\n4. `NotAcceptingNewRequest` signal fires → new requests get 429 with `Retry-After` (if `ShutdownSendRetryAfter` is true).\n5. In-flight non-long-running requests drain → `InFlightRequestsDrained` signal fires.\n6. Watch connections terminate (bounded by `ShutdownWatchTerminationGracePeriod`).\n7. HTTP server closes with a final `ShutdownTimeout`.\n8. `Destroy()` cleans up storage connections.\n\n**Risk:** If `ShutdownDelayDuration` is too short, load balancers may still route traffic to the shutting-down server, causing client errors. If it's too long, rolling updates are slower.\n\n---\n\n## 5. Extension Points, Customization Hooks, and Associated Risks\n\n### 5.1 `BuildHandlerChainFunc`\n\n**Location:** `Config.BuildHandlerChainFunc` (`config.go`, field on `Config` struct ~line 186)\n\n**What it does:** Allows replacing the entire filter chain. The default is `DefaultBuildHandlerChain`. A custom function receives the API handler and `*Config` and must return an `http.Handler`.\n\n**Use case:** Adding custom authentication, injecting request-scoped metadata, or adding custom rate limiting.\n\n**Risk:** Replacing the chain means the operator is responsible for including all security-critical filters (authentication, authorization, audit). Omitting `WithAuthorization` would create an unauthenticated API server. Omitting `WithPanicRecovery` could crash the process on handler panics.\n\n### 5.2 PostStartHooks and PreShutdownHooks\n\n**Location:** `GenericAPIServer.AddPostStartHook()` (`hooks.go:83`), `AddPreShutdownHook()`\n\n**What they do:** PostStartHooks run in separate goroutines after the server begins listening. They receive a `PostStartHookContext` with a loopback client config. Each hook has an associated health check—the server is not healthy until all hooks complete.\n\n**Use case:** Initializing controllers that need the server's own API (e.g., populating discovery, starting informers). The kube-apiserver uses these extensively to bootstrap controllers.\n\n**Risk:** A hook that blocks or panics will either keep the server unhealthy (blocking readiness) or terminate the process (`hooks.go:195-206` runs with crash recovery that fatals on error). Hooks run concurrently with no ordering guarantees, so inter-hook dependencies must be coordinated externally (e.g., via channels or informer cache syncs).\n\n### 5.3 Admission Plugin Registration\n\n**Location:** `admission.Interface` (`admission/interfaces.go:123`), wired via `Config.AdmissionControl`\n\n**What it does:** The admission chain is fully pluggable. Custom plugins implement `MutationInterface`, `ValidationInterface`, or both. They are composed into a `chainAdmissionHandler` (`admission/chain.go:23`).\n\n**Use case:** Enforcing custom business rules, injecting sidecars, validating naming conventions.\n\n**Risk:** Mutating plugins run in order, and later plugins see earlier mutations. This creates implicit coupling between plugins. A mutating plugin that modifies a field validated by a subsequent validating plugin can cause unexpected rejections. The admission chain is also single-threaded per request—a slow plugin blocks the entire request pipeline.\n\n### 5.4 StorageDecorator\n\n**Location:** `StorageDecorator` function type (`registry/generic/storage_decorator.go:27`), passed via `RESTOptions.Decorator`\n\n**What it does:** Wraps storage creation. The default `StorageWithCacher()` (`registry/generic/registry/storage_factory.go:36`) adds the `Cacher` watch cache layer. Custom decorators could add encryption, auditing, or custom caching.\n\n**Use case:** The encryption-at-rest feature uses a `value.Transformer` passed through the storage config rather than the decorator, but the decorator pattern could wrap storage with custom metrics or tracing.\n\n**Risk:** A decorator that introduces latency on the write path directly impacts API response times. A decorator that caches writes without proper invalidation can cause split-brain between what etcd holds and what the API returns.\n\n### 5.5 REST Strategy Interfaces\n\n**Location:** `rest.RESTCreateStrategy`, `rest.RESTUpdateStrategy`, `rest.RESTDeleteStrategy` (defined in `registry/rest/`)\n\n**What they do:** These interfaces allow resource-specific logic to plug into the generic `Store`. Methods like `PrepareForCreate`, `Validate`, `PrepareForUpdate`, and `ValidateUpdate` are called at well-defined points in the CRUD lifecycle.\n\n**Use case:** Every built-in resource (Pod, Deployment, Service, etc.) implements these to enforce its own invariants.\n\n**Risk:** Strategy implementations that are too expensive (e.g., deep-copying large objects unnecessarily, running expensive validation) degrade API latency. The `Store` invokes strategies synchronously and does not set per-strategy timeouts.\n\n### 5.6 DelegationTarget Chain\n\n**Location:** `DelegationTarget` interface (`genericapiserver.go:308`), `GenericAPIServer.delegationTarget` field\n\n**What it does:** Enables composing multiple API servers into a chain. The kube-apiserver binary composes three servers: `apiextensions-apiserver` → `kube-apiserver` → `aggregator`. Each server in the chain installs its own API groups and contributes hooks and health checks.\n\nThe `UnprotectedHandler()` method (`genericapiserver.go:339`) returns the delegate's `Director`, allowing the outer server to route unmatched requests to the inner server without re-applying the filter chain.\n\n**Use case:** The aggregator server proxies requests for aggregated API services to their backing API servers. The CRD server (apiextensions) dynamically installs and removes routes as CRDs are created and deleted.\n\n**Risk:** Delegation introduces a request forwarding hop. If the delegate is slow, the outer server's timeout applies. Misconfigured delegation (e.g., two servers claiming the same API group) results in route conflicts and undefined behavior.\n\n### 5.7 The `Decorator` Field on `Store`\n\n**Location:** `Store.Decorator` (`registry/generic/registry/store.go:170`)\n\n**What it does:** An optional function called on every object returned from storage (both individual gets and list items). Unlike storage decorators, this runs *after* persistence, on the returned object.\n\n**Use case:** Adding computed fields that aren't persisted (e.g., a node's allocatable resources derived from capacity minus reservations).\n\n**Risk:** Decorators cannot be watched—the watch stream delivers objects without decoration. This creates an inconsistency between GET and WATCH responses. The docstring explicitly warns about this limitation.\n\n### 5.8 `BeginCreate` / `BeginUpdate` Transaction Hooks\n\n**Location:** `Store.BeginCreate` (`store.go:179`), `Store.BeginUpdate` (`store.go:191`)\n\n**What they do:** Return a commit/revert function that is called at the end of the operation, indicating success or failure. This provides a transaction-like pattern for operations that need side-effects coordinated with persistence.\n\n**Use case:** Allocating IPs during Service creation—if the etcd write fails, the IP allocation is reverted.\n\n**Risk:** The hook runs before `AfterCreate` and `Decorator`. If the commit function has side effects that depend on external state (e.g., an IP allocator), failures in the commit function can leave the system in an inconsistent state.\n\n---\n\n## 6. Operational Implications\n\n### 6.1 Performance\n\n**Watch scalability** is the single most important performance characteristic. The `Cacher` fan-out architecture means that adding watchers is O(1) with respect to etcd load—each additional watcher only adds a `cacheWatcher` goroutine and a channel to the dispatch loop. However, the dispatch loop (`cacher.go`, dispatching logic) holds the `Cacher` lock while iterating watchers, so very high watcher counts (tens of thousands) can create lock contention. The `indexedWatchers` map (`cacher.go:309`) optimizes dispatch by pre-indexing watchers by trigger value, so only watchers matching an event's trigger are considered.\n\n**APF queue depth** directly impacts tail latency. When a priority level's concurrency limit is reached, requests queue. The queue's `HandSize` and `Queues` parameters in the FlowSchema determine fairness characteristics. Misconfiguration (e.g., too few queues) can cause shuffle-sharding hot-spots.\n\n**Serialization cost** is non-trivial for large list responses. The negotiation layer (`handlers/negotiation/negotiate.go`) selects the codec. Protobuf is significantly faster than JSON for large payloads. The `WatchServer` (`watch.go:188`) allocates a `MemoryAllocator` per watch to reduce GC pressure from repeated serialization.\n\n### 6.2 Reliability\n\n**etcd connectivity loss** is the primary single-point-of-failure scenario. The `Cacher` continues serving reads from cache during etcd outages, but writes fail immediately. The `Reflector` backing the cache enters backoff retry. The storage readiness check (`StorageReadinessHook` at `genericapiserver.go:245`, registered via `registerStorageReadinessCheck` at `genericapiserver.go:934`) can signal unreadiness, but this is informational—the server does not self-terminate.\n\n**Request body limits** (`maxRequestBodyBytes` on `GenericAPIServer`) protect against memory exhaustion from oversized payloads. The default is typically 3 MB. Without this, a single malicious POST could OOM the process.\n\n**Panic recovery** (`filters/wrap.go:31`) catches panics in handlers and returns 500 errors rather than crashing. However, panics in filter-chain code *above* the panic recovery filter (e.g., in `WithAuditInit`) will terminate the process.\n\n### 6.3 Maintainability\n\nThe library's layered architecture (filters → routing → handlers → storage) makes it possible to modify individual layers independently. However, several maintainability concerns exist:\n\n- **go-restful coupling:** The `Director` (`handler.go:42`) comment explicitly notes the desire to \"completely remove gorestful.\" The dual-path routing (GoRestful vs. NonGoRestful) adds complexity and subtle behavior differences (e.g., 404 handling, content negotiation).\n- **Filter ordering sensitivity:** The handler chain in `DefaultBuildHandlerChain()` is order-dependent. Authorization must come after authentication. Timeout must come before the handler that might block. Moving a filter can create security vulnerabilities or correctness bugs, and there are no compile-time guarantees on ordering.\n- **Storage interface breadth:** `storage.Interface` (`storage/interfaces.go:169`) has grown to 12+ methods including `CompactRevision()`, `EnableResourceSizeEstimation()`, and `GetCurrentResourceVersion()`. The interface comment acknowledges this is not ideal (`TODO: Remove when storage.Interface will be separate from etc3.store`).\n\n---\n\n## 7. Subsystem Purpose and Boundaries\n\nThe `apiserver` library (`staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/`) is a reusable framework for building Kubernetes-style API servers. It provides the full HTTP request lifecycle—authentication, authorization, admission control, serialization, REST semantics, storage, and watch—as composable Go packages. The `kube-apiserver` binary is the primary consumer, but the library is intentionally decoupled so that projects like the aggregated API server, CRD API server, and custom API servers built with `apiserver-builder` can embed and extend it independently.\n\n### Boundaries\n\nThe library owns everything *between* the TLS listener and the etcd client. It does **not** own:\n\n- **Upstream:** TLS certificate management, load-balancer health probing, or network policy. These are external to the process.\n- **Downstream:** The etcd cluster itself. The library provides an etcd3 storage driver (`pkg/storage/etcd3/`) but treats etcd as a pluggable backend behind the `storage.Interface` abstraction (`pkg/storage/interfaces.go:169`).\n- **Peer concerns:** Controller logic, scheduler decisions, and kubelet communication. The API server library is strictly a data-plane gateway for the cluster's persisted state.\n\n### Upstream Dependencies\n\n| Dependency | Role |\n|---|---|\n| `k8s.io/apimachinery` | Shared type system (`runtime.Object`, `schema.GroupVersionKind`), serialization codecs, field selectors, label selectors |\n| `k8s.io/client-go` | Loopback client for self-referential operations (post-start hooks use `LoopbackClientConfig`) |\n| `go.etcd.io/etcd/client/v3` | etcd gRPC client used by `pkg/storage/etcd3/store.go` |\n| `github.com/emicklei/go-restful/v3` | HTTP routing framework for API group endpoints |\n| `k8s.io/kube-openapi` | OpenAPI v2/v3 spec generation and serving |\n\n### Downstream Consumers\n\nAny binary that calls `GenericAPIServer.InstallAPIGroups()` to register resources. The canonical example is `cmd/kube-apiserver`, but the library is also used by the aggregator (`kube-aggregator`) and sample API servers.\n\n---\n\n## 2. Key Components and Responsibility Split\n\nThe library decomposes into six major subsystems. Each has a clear responsibility boundary and communicates with neighbors through well-defined Go interfaces.\n\n### 2.1 Server Core (`pkg/server/`)\n\n**Responsibility:** Assembles the HTTP handler chain, manages server lifecycle (start, readiness, graceful shutdown), and provides the delegation mechanism for composing multiple API servers.\n\n**Key types:**\n\n- `GenericAPIServer` (`genericapiserver.go:109`): The central server struct. Holds the handler, admission controller, authorizer, post-start hooks, health checks, lifecycle signals, and the delegation target chain.\n- `Config` (`config.go:110`): Configuration for building a `GenericAPIServer`. Contains `BuildHandlerChainFunc`, authentication/authorization info, flow control settings, shutdown parameters, and the `RESTOptionsGetter` for storage configuration.\n- `APIServerHandler` (`handler.go:42`): Wraps three HTTP handler tiers: `FullHandlerChain` (all filters applied), `GoRestfulContainer` (API routes), and `NonGoRestfulMux` (non-API routes like `/healthz`, `/metrics`). The `Director` (`handler.go:115`) routes between the two backends.\n- `DelegationTarget` interface (`genericapiserver.go:308`): Enables chaining of multiple API servers (e.g., kube-apiserver delegates to aggregator delegates to apiextensions-server). Each delegate contributes its own hooks, health checks, and unprotected handlers.\n\n### 2.2 Filter Chain (`pkg/server/filters/`, `pkg/endpoints/filters/`)\n\n**Responsibility:** Implements the ordered chain of HTTP middleware that every request passes through before reaching the REST handler.\n\nThese are pure `http.Handler` wrappers composed in `DefaultBuildHandlerChain()` (`config.go:1015`). The chain is assembled inside-out (innermost handler wraps first), so the outermost filter in the source code is the first to execute at runtime.\n\nFilter files are split across two packages:\n- `pkg/server/filters/` — infrastructure filters (panic recovery, timeouts, flow control, CORS, GOAWAY)\n- `pkg/endpoints/filters/` — API-semantic filters (authentication, authorization, audit, impersonation, request info)\n\n### 2.3 Endpoint Handlers (`pkg/endpoints/`)\n\n**Responsibility:** Maps REST verbs to handler functions, installs API group routes into the go-restful container, and drives content negotiation.\n\n- `APIInstaller` (`installer.go:62`): Given an `APIGroupVersion` with a storage map, generates go-restful `WebService` routes for every resource. The central function `registerResourceHandlers()` (`installer.go:287`) introspects which `rest.*` interfaces each storage implements (e.g., `rest.Creater`, `rest.Lister`, `rest.Watcher`) and registers only the supported verbs.\n- Verb handlers in `pkg/endpoints/handlers/`: `GetResource()` / `ListResource()` (`get.go`), `CreateResource()` (`create.go`), `UpdateResource()` (`update.go`), `PatchResource()` (`patch.go`), `DeleteResource()` / `DeleteCollection()` (`delete.go`), `WatchServer` (`watch.go`).\n- Content negotiation (`handlers/negotiation/negotiate.go`): Matches `Accept` / `Content-Type` headers to registered serializers (JSON, YAML, Protobuf, CBOR).\n\n### 2.4 Admission Control (`pkg/admission/`)\n\n**Responsibility:** Runs pluggable mutation and validation logic on create, update, and delete operations after authentication and authorization but before persistence.\n\n- `Interface` / `MutationInterface` / `ValidationInterface` (`interfaces.go:123-144`): The core plugin interfaces. A plugin can implement mutation, validation, or both.\n- `chainAdmissionHandler` (`chain.go:23`): Chains multiple plugins. `Admit()` runs all mutating plugins in order, short-circuiting on error. `Validate()` runs all validating plugins and aggregates errors.\n- Admission is invoked inside endpoint handlers. For example, in `CreateResource()` (`create.go`), mutating admission runs at line ~203 via `mutatingAdmission.Admit()`, and validating admission is wired through `rest.AdmissionToValidateObjectFunc()`.\n\n### 2.5 Authentication & Authorization (`pkg/authentication/`, `pkg/authorization/`, `pkg/endpoints/filters/`)\n\n**Responsibility:** Establish caller identity and enforce access policy.\n\n- **Authentication filter** (`endpoints/filters/authentication.go:46`): `WithAuthentication()` calls `authenticator.Request.AuthenticateRequest()`, stores the resulting `user.Info` in the request context, and strips the `Authorization` header. If authentication fails, the request is forwarded to a `failedHandler` that returns 401.\n- **Authorization filter** (`endpoints/filters/authorization.go:53`): `WithAuthorization()` constructs `AttributesRecord` from the request info and user, calls `authorizer.Authorize()`, and returns 403 on `DecisionDeny` or `DecisionNoOpinion`. The `Authorizer` interface (`authorization/authorizer/interfaces.go:83`) returns a three-valued decision: `DecisionAllow`, `DecisionDeny`, `DecisionNoOpinion`.\n\n### 2.6 Storage Layer (`pkg/storage/`, `pkg/registry/`)\n\n**Responsibility:** Provides a key-value abstraction over etcd and an in-memory watch cache for serving list and watch requests efficiently.\n\n- `storage.Interface` (`storage/interfaces.go:169`): The backend contract. Methods: `Create`, `Delete`, `Watch`, `Get`, `GetList`, `GuaranteedUpdate`. Implementations do not know about Kubernetes resource semantics—they operate on opaque keys and `runtime.Object`.\n- `etcd3.store` (`storage/etcd3/store.go:80`): Direct etcd3 implementation. Handles codec transformations, lease management, and value encryption via a configurable `value.Transformer`.\n- `Cacher` (`storage/cacher/cacher.go:262`): In-memory cache that fronts the etcd3 store. Serves `Watch` and `List` from a ring-buffer `watchCache` populated by a `Reflector`. Mutations are delegated to the underlying `storage.Interface`. This is the component that makes watch scalable—without it, every watch would be a direct etcd watch, which does not scale past a few hundred concurrent watchers.\n- `Store` (`registry/generic/registry/store.go:100`): The generic REST storage implementation that most built-in resources embed. Implements CRUD by composing `storage.Interface` with resource-specific strategies (`RESTCreateStrategy`, `RESTUpdateStrategy`, `RESTDeleteStrategy`).\n- `StorageDecorator` (`registry/generic/storage_decorator.go:27`): A function type that wraps raw storage creation. The default decorator is `StorageWithCacher()` (`registry/generic/registry/storage_factory.go:36`), which wraps etcd3 storage with the `Cacher`.\n\n---\n\n## 3. End-to-End Request Flow\n\nThis section traces a `POST /apis/apps/v1/namespaces/default/deployments` request (creating a Deployment) through the full apiserver code path, citing the exact points where control transfers.\n\n### Phase 1: Filter Chain\n\nThe request enters `APIServerHandler.ServeHTTP()` (`handler.go:187`), which delegates to `FullHandlerChain`. The chain was assembled by `DefaultBuildHandlerChain()` (`config.go:1015`). Filters execute in the following order (outermost first at runtime):\n\n```\n1. WithAuditInit                              (config.go:1095)\n2. WithPanicRecovery                          (config.go:1094)\n3. WithMuxAndDiscoveryComplete                (config.go:1093)\n4. WithRequestReceivedTimestamp               (config.go:1092)\n5. WithRequestInfo                            (config.go:1091)\n   → Parses the URL into RequestInfo (verb=create, resource=deployments,\n     namespace=default, apiGroup=apps, apiVersion=v1)\n6. WithRoutine (conditional)                  (config.go:1089)\n7. WithLatencyTrackers                        (config.go:1084)\n8. WithHTTPLogging                            (config.go:1083)\n9. WithRetryAfter (conditional, shutdown)     (config.go:1081)\n10. WithHSTS                                  (config.go:1079)\n11. WithCacheControl                          (config.go:1078)\n12. WithProbabilisticGoaway (conditional)     (config.go:1076)\n13. WithWatchTerminationDuringShutdown        (config.go:1073)\n14. WithWaitGroup                             (config.go:1071)\n    → Increments NonLongRunningRequestWaitGroup so graceful\n      shutdown knows this request is in flight.\n15. WithRequestDeadline                       (config.go:1069)\n16. WithTimeoutForNonLongRunningRequests      (config.go:1067)\n    → Sets a context deadline. The handler runs in a goroutine;\n      if it exceeds the timeout, a 504 is returned to the client.\n17. WithWarningRecorder                       (config.go:1063)\n18. WithCORS                                  (config.go:1059)\n19. WithAuthentication                        (config.go:1056)\n    → Calls authenticator.Request.AuthenticateRequest(). On success,\n      stores user.Info in context. On failure, delegates to\n      failedHandler (401 with audit event).\n20. WithTracing (conditional)                 (config.go:1052)\n21. WithAudit                                 (config.go:1043)\n    → Creates audit event, evaluates policy rules, and ensures the\n      event is emitted at response time.\n22. WithImpersonation / WithConstrainedImpersonation  (config.go:1035-1039)\n23. WithPriorityAndFairness / WithMaxInFlightLimit     (config.go:1022-1031)\n    → If APF is enabled, classifies the request into a FlowSchema\n      and PriorityLevel, potentially queuing it. Otherwise, enforces\n      simple concurrency limits (MaxRequestsInFlight /\n      MaxMutatingRequestsInFlight).\n24. WithAuthorization                         (config.go:1019)\n    → Calls authorizer.Authorize(). Returns 403 if not allowed.\n```\n\n### Phase 2: Routing (Director)\n\nAfter the filter chain, control reaches the `director.ServeHTTP()` method (`handler.go:121`). The director iterates over registered `go-restful` WebServices. For our request path `/apis/apps/v1/namespaces/default/deployments`, it matches a WebService rooted at `/apis/apps/v1` and dispatches via `goRestfulContainer.Dispatch()` (`handler.go:145`).\n\nIf no WebService matches (e.g., `/healthz`, `/metrics`), the request falls through to `NonGoRestfulMux` (`handler.go:153`).\n\n### Phase 3: REST Handler Execution\n\nThe go-restful container matches the route to the handler installed by `registerResourceHandlers()` (`installer.go:287`). For a POST, this is `restfulCreateResource()` (`installer.go:1306`), which wraps `CreateResource()` (`create.go:245`).\n\nInside `CreateResource()`:\n\n1. **Decode the request body** (create.go, ~line 100-140): Uses the negotiated serializer based on `Content-Type`. The object is deserialized into an internal `runtime.Object`.\n\n2. **Default and validate** (via `CreateStrategy`): The `RESTCreateStrategy` interface (defined in `registry/rest/`) calls `PrepareForCreate`, `Validate`, and `Canonicalize` on the object.\n\n3. **Mutating admission** (~line 203): If the admission controller implements `MutationInterface`, `Admit()` is called. This runs the entire chain of mutating admission plugins (including webhooks) in sequence. Each plugin can modify the object.\n\n4. **Validating admission** (~line 188): `Validate()` runs all validating admission plugins. Errors from all plugins are aggregated and returned.\n\n5. **Field management** (via `FieldManager`, ~line 199): For server-side apply and managed-field tracking, the field manager updates ownership metadata.\n\n6. **Persist to storage**: The handler calls `rest.NamedCreater.Create()`, which resolves to `Store.Create()` (`registry/generic/registry/store.go`). The `Store` constructs the etcd key using `KeyFunc`, then calls `storage.Interface.Create()`.\n\n### Phase 4: Storage Write Path\n\n`storage.Interface.Create()` reaches either the `Cacher` or the raw `etcd3.store`, depending on the decorator.\n\nWhen using the standard `StorageWithCacher()` decorator:\n- **Create goes directly to etcd**: `Cacher` delegates mutations to the underlying `etcd3.store.Create()` (`storage/etcd3/store.go`). The etcd3 implementation encodes the object, applies any configured `value.Transformer` (e.g., encryption at rest), and issues an etcd `PUT` with a lease if TTL is specified.\n- **The Cacher's watch cache is updated asynchronously**: A separate goroutine running a `Reflector` watches etcd for changes and pushes events into the `Cacher.incoming` channel, which are then dispatched to all registered `cacheWatcher` instances.\n\n### Phase 5: Response Serialization\n\nAfter successful persistence, the handler serializes the created object using the negotiated output serializer, sets appropriate HTTP status (201 Created), and writes it to the `http.ResponseWriter`. The filter chain then unwinds—audit events are finalized, wait groups are decremented, and latency metrics are recorded.\n\n### Watch Flow (Variant)\n\nFor `GET /api/v1/pods?watch=true`, `ListResource()` (`get.go:171`) detects `opts.Watch == true` at line ~250, calls `rw.Watch()` on the storage to obtain a `watch.Interface`, and hands it to `serveWatchHandler()` (`watch.go:70`). This creates a `WatchServer` (`watch.go:188`) that enters a long-running loop (`HandleHTTP()`, watch.go:235):\n\n```\nfor {\n    select {\n    case event := <-watcher.ResultChan():\n        encode and flush event to HTTP response\n    case <-serverShuttingDown:\n        return\n    case <-ctx.Done():\n        return\n    case <-timeout:\n        return\n    }\n}\n```\n\nEvents arrive from `Cacher.Watch()`, which creates a `cacheWatcher` (`storage/cacher/cache_watcher.go:53`) that filters the shared event stream by the watch's predicate. This fan-out architecture means thousands of watchers share a single etcd watch per resource type.\n\n---\n\n## 4. Failure Modes, Limits, and Design Tradeoffs\n\n### 4.1 Watch Cache Consistency\n\nThe `Cacher` serves list and watch from an in-memory cache that lags behind etcd by an indeterminate amount. This is a deliberate tradeoff: serving from cache avoids overwhelming etcd with read traffic, but clients can observe stale data.\n\n**Mitigation:** The `ResourceVersion` mechanism provides consistency control. Clients can request `resourceVersion=0` (serve from cache, any version) or `resourceVersion=\"\"` (quorum read from etcd). The `Cacher` tracks the `incomingHWM` (high water mark, `cacher.go:266`) to determine the freshest version available in cache. Bookmark events (`cacheWatcher` states at `cache_watcher.go:37-49`) keep long-running watches informed of progress even when no real events occur.\n\n**Risk:** If the reflector falls behind or is disconnected, the cache may serve increasingly stale data. The `ready` flag (`cacher.go:280`) blocks reads during cache repopulation to prevent serving partial state.\n\n### 4.2 Admission Webhook Failure\n\nMutating and validating admission webhooks are external HTTP calls. If a webhook endpoint is unreachable:\n\n- **Fail-open vs. fail-closed** is configured per webhook via `failurePolicy`. A `Fail` policy rejects the request; an `Ignore` policy allows it to proceed without webhook evaluation.\n- **Timeout:** Webhooks have a configurable timeout (default 10s). A slow webhook blocks the entire request.\n\n**Tradeoff:** Fail-closed provides stronger policy enforcement but can cause cascading unavailability if the webhook backend is down—potentially blocking all mutations in the cluster. Fail-open preserves availability but allows policy violations to slip through.\n\n### 4.3 Request Timeout and Long-Running Requests\n\n`WithTimeoutForNonLongRunningRequests` (`filters/timeout.go:38`) enforces a deadline on regular requests. Long-running requests (watches, port-forwards, exec) are identified by `LongRunningFunc` (`filters/longrunning.go:28`) based on verb and subresource and are **exempted** from this timeout.\n\n**Tradeoff:** Timeout exemption for watches means a misbehaving watch can consume a connection and goroutine indefinitely. The `WithWatchTerminationDuringShutdown` filter (`filters/watch_termination.go:28`) addresses this during graceful shutdown by tracking watches in a wait group and terminating them after a grace period. The `WatchRequestWaitGroup` (`genericapiserver.go:228`) uses rate-limited termination to avoid thundering-herd reconnects.\n\n### 4.4 Priority and Fairness (APF) vs. Max-In-Flight\n\nThe server supports two concurrency control mechanisms, selected by whether `FlowControl` is configured (`config.go:1022-1031`):\n\n- **APF** (`filters/priority-and-fairness.go`): Classifies requests into FlowSchemas mapped to PriorityLevels, each with dedicated concurrency shares and queuing. This prevents a burst of low-priority requests (e.g., a runaway controller list-all) from starving high-priority requests (e.g., node heartbeats).\n- **Max-In-Flight** (`filters/maxinflight.go:126`): Simple counting semaphore with separate limits for mutating and read-only requests. No queuing—excess requests get 429.\n\n**Tradeoff:** APF provides fairness but adds complexity and latency (queue wait time). Max-In-Flight is simpler but provides no isolation between tenants or request classes.\n\n### 4.5 etcd Storage Pressure\n\nEvery mutating request results in an etcd write. The `GuaranteedUpdate` method (`storage/interfaces.go:243`) retries on conflict (stale `resourceVersion`), which can amplify write load under contention. The etcd3 store maintains leases for TTL objects and runs a compactor to reclaim space.\n\n**Limit:** etcd has a default 1.5 MB value size limit and a recommended database size of 8 GB. Large objects (e.g., very large ConfigMaps, deeply nested CRDs) can hit the value size limit. The `maxRequestBodyBytes` field on `GenericAPIServer` (`genericapiserver.go:238`) bounds request body sizes server-side.\n\n### 4.6 Graceful Shutdown Sequence\n\nThe shutdown flow (`genericapiserver.go:525-624`) is multi-phased:\n\n1. `stopCh` is closed → `ShutdownInitiated` signal fires → `/readyz` starts returning failure.\n2. `ShutdownDelayDuration` elapses → `AfterShutdownDelayDuration` signal fires → load balancers should have drained.\n3. Pre-shutdown hooks execute.\n4. `NotAcceptingNewRequest` signal fires → new requests get 429 with `Retry-After` (if `ShutdownSendRetryAfter` is true).\n5. In-flight non-long-running requests drain → `InFlightRequestsDrained` signal fires.\n6. Watch connections terminate (bounded by `ShutdownWatchTerminationGracePeriod`).\n7. HTTP server closes with a final `ShutdownTimeout`.\n8. `Destroy()` cleans up storage connections.\n\n**Risk:** If `ShutdownDelayDuration` is too short, load balancers may still route traffic to the shutting-down server, causing client errors. If it's too long, rolling updates are slower.\n\n---\n\n## 5. Extension Points, Customization Hooks, and Associated Risks\n\n### 5.1 `BuildHandlerChainFunc`\n\n**Location:** `Config.BuildHandlerChainFunc` (`config.go`, field on `Config` struct ~line 186)\n\n**What it does:** Allows replacing the entire filter chain. The default is `DefaultBuildHandlerChain`. A custom function receives the API handler and `*Config` and must return an `http.Handler`.\n\n**Use case:** Adding custom authentication, injecting request-scoped metadata, or adding custom rate limiting.\n\n**Risk:** Replacing the chain means the operator is responsible for including all security-critical filters (authentication, authorization, audit). Omitting `WithAuthorization` would create an unauthenticated API server. Omitting `WithPanicRecovery` could crash the process on handler panics.\n\n### 5.2 PostStartHooks and PreShutdownHooks\n\n**Location:** `GenericAPIServer.AddPostStartHook()` (`hooks.go:83`), `AddPreShutdownHook()`\n\n**What they do:** PostStartHooks run in separate goroutines after the server begins listening. They receive a `PostStartHookContext` with a loopback client config. Each hook has an associated health check—the server is not healthy until all hooks complete.\n\n**Use case:** Initializing controllers that need the server's own API (e.g., populating discovery, starting informers). The kube-apiserver uses these extensively to bootstrap controllers.\n\n**Risk:** A hook that blocks or panics will either keep the server unhealthy (blocking readiness) or terminate the process (`hooks.go:195-206` runs with crash recovery that fatals on error). Hooks run concurrently with no ordering guarantees, so inter-hook dependencies must be coordinated externally (e.g., via channels or informer cache syncs).\n\n### 5.3 Admission Plugin Registration\n\n**Location:** `admission.Interface` (`admission/interfaces.go:123`), wired via `Config.AdmissionControl`\n\n**What it does:** The admission chain is fully pluggable. Custom plugins implement `MutationInterface`, `ValidationInterface`, or both. They are composed into a `chainAdmissionHandler` (`admission/chain.go:23`).\n\n**Use case:** Enforcing custom business rules, injecting sidecars, validating naming conventions.\n\n**Risk:** Mutating plugins run in order, and later plugins see earlier mutations. This creates implicit coupling between plugins. A mutating plugin that modifies a field validated by a subsequent validating plugin can cause unexpected rejections. The admission chain is also single-threaded per request—a slow plugin blocks the entire request pipeline.\n\n### 5.4 StorageDecorator\n\n**Location:** `StorageDecorator` function type (`registry/generic/storage_decorator.go:27`), passed via `RESTOptions.Decorator`\n\n**What it does:** Wraps storage creation. The default `StorageWithCacher()` (`registry/generic/registry/storage_factory.go:36`) adds the `Cacher` watch cache layer. Custom decorators could add encryption, auditing, or custom caching.\n\n**Use case:** The encryption-at-rest feature uses a `value.Transformer` passed through the storage config rather than the decorator, but the decorator pattern could wrap storage with custom metrics or tracing.\n\n**Risk:** A decorator that introduces latency on the write path directly impacts API response times. A decorator that caches writes without proper invalidation can cause split-brain between what etcd holds and what the API returns.\n\n### 5.5 REST Strategy Interfaces\n\n**Location:** `rest.RESTCreateStrategy`, `rest.RESTUpdateStrategy`, `rest.RESTDeleteStrategy` (defined in `registry/rest/`)\n\n**What they do:** These interfaces allow resource-specific logic to plug into the generic `Store`. Methods like `PrepareForCreate`, `Validate`, `PrepareForUpdate`, and `ValidateUpdate` are called at well-defined points in the CRUD lifecycle.\n\n**Use case:** Every built-in resource (Pod, Deployment, Service, etc.) implements these to enforce its own invariants.\n\n**Risk:** Strategy implementations that are too expensive (e.g., deep-copying large objects unnecessarily, running expensive validation) degrade API latency. The `Store` invokes strategies synchronously and does not set per-strategy timeouts.\n\n### 5.6 DelegationTarget Chain\n\n**Location:** `DelegationTarget` interface (`genericapiserver.go:308`), `GenericAPIServer.delegationTarget` field\n\n**What it does:** Enables composing multiple API servers into a chain. The kube-apiserver binary composes three servers: `apiextensions-apiserver` → `kube-apiserver` → `aggregator`. Each server in the chain installs its own API groups and contributes hooks and health checks.\n\nThe `UnprotectedHandler()` method (`genericapiserver.go:339`) returns the delegate's `Director`, allowing the outer server to route unmatched requests to the inner server without re-applying the filter chain.\n\n**Use case:** The aggregator server proxies requests for aggregated API services to their backing API servers. The CRD server (apiextensions) dynamically installs and removes routes as CRDs are created and deleted.\n\n**Risk:** Delegation introduces a request forwarding hop. If the delegate is slow, the outer server's timeout applies. Misconfigured delegation (e.g., two servers claiming the same API group) results in route conflicts and undefined behavior.\n\n### 5.7 The `Decorator` Field on `Store`\n\n**Location:** `Store.Decorator` (`registry/generic/registry/store.go:170`)\n\n**What it does:** An optional function called on every object returned from storage (both individual gets and list items). Unlike storage decorators, this runs *after* persistence, on the returned object.\n\n**Use case:** Adding computed fields that aren't persisted (e.g., a node's allocatable resources derived from capacity minus reservations).\n\n**Risk:** Decorators cannot be watched—the watch stream delivers objects without decoration. This creates an inconsistency between GET and WATCH responses. The docstring explicitly warns about this limitation.\n\n### 5.8 `BeginCreate` / `BeginUpdate` Transaction Hooks\n\n**Location:** `Store.BeginCreate` (`store.go:179`), `Store.BeginUpdate` (`store.go:191`)\n\n**What they do:** Return a commit/revert function that is called at the end of the operation, indicating success or failure. This provides a transaction-like pattern for operations that need side-effects coordinated with persistence.\n\n**Use case:** Allocating IPs during Service creation—if the etcd write fails, the IP allocation is reverted.\n\n**Risk:** The hook runs before `AfterCreate` and `Decorator`. If the commit function has side effects that depend on external state (e.g., an IP allocator), failures in the commit function can leave the system in an inconsistent state.\n\n---\n\n## 6. Operational Implications\n\n### 6.1 Performance\n\n**Watch scalability** is the single most important performance characteristic. The `Cacher` fan-out architecture means that adding watchers is O(1) with respect to etcd load—each additional watcher only adds a `cacheWatcher` goroutine and a channel to the dispatch loop. However, the dispatch loop (`cacher.go`, dispatching logic) holds the `Cacher` lock while iterating watchers, so very high watcher counts (tens of thousands) can create lock contention. The `indexedWatchers` map (`cacher.go:309`) optimizes dispatch by pre-indexing watchers by trigger value, so only watchers matching an event's trigger are considered.\n\n**APF queue depth** directly impacts tail latency. When a priority level's concurrency limit is reached, requests queue. The queue's `HandSize` and `Queues` parameters in the FlowSchema determine fairness characteristics. Misconfiguration (e.g., too few queues) can cause shuffle-sharding hot-spots.\n\n**Serialization cost** is non-trivial for large list responses. The negotiation layer (`handlers/negotiation/negotiate.go`) selects the codec. Protobuf is significantly faster than JSON for large payloads. The `WatchServer` (`watch.go:188`) allocates a `MemoryAllocator` per watch to reduce GC pressure from repeated serialization.\n\n### 6.2 Reliability\n\n**etcd connectivity loss** is the primary single-point-of-failure scenario. The `Cacher` continues serving reads from cache during etcd outages, but writes fail immediately. The `Reflector` backing the cache enters backoff retry. The storage readiness check (`StorageReadinessHook` at `genericapiserver.go:245`, registered via `registerStorageReadinessCheck` at `genericapiserver.go:934`) can signal unreadiness, but this is informational—the server does not self-terminate.\n\n**Request body limits** (`maxRequestBodyBytes` on `GenericAPIServer`) protect against memory exhaustion from oversized payloads. The default is typically 3 MB. Without this, a single malicious POST could OOM the process.\n\n**Panic recovery** (`filters/wrap.go:31`) catches panics in handlers and returns 500 errors rather than crashing. However, panics in filter-chain code *above* the panic recovery filter (e.g., in `WithAuditInit`) will terminate the process.\n\n### 6.3 Maintainability\n\nThe library's layered architecture (filters → routing → handlers → storage) makes it possible to modify individual layers independently. However, several maintainability concerns exist:\n\n- **go-restful coupling:** The `Director` (`handler.go:42`) comment explicitly notes the desire to \"completely remove gorestful.\" The dual-path routing (GoRestful vs. NonGoRestful) adds complexity and subtle behavior differences (e.g., 404 handling, content negotiation).\n- **Filter ordering sensitivity:** The handler chain in `DefaultBuildHandlerChain()` is order-dependent. Authorization must come after authentication. Timeout must come before the handler that might block. Moving a filter can create security vulnerabilities or correctness bugs, and there are no compile-time guarantees on ordering.\n- **Storage interface breadth:** `storage.Interface` (`storage/interfaces.go:169`) has grown to 12+ methods including `CompactRevision()`, `EnableResourceSizeEstimation()`, and `GetCurrentResourceVersion()`. The interface comment acknowledges this is not ideal (`TODO: Remove when storage.Interface will be separate from etc3.store`).\n\n---\n\n## 7.
